messages.subject: comparing density estimates
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have to compare density estimates from LTsurveys carried out from 2001 to
2006.

May I use an Anova test?

If yes, is it correct calculating the grand mean (weighted average) using the
degree of freedom of each estimate? (if not, how can I calculate the
"sample size" of the density estimate?)

If not, which analysis is better to use?

I'd really appreciate any suggestion (reference to papers, books...) you all may
give.

Thanks,

Barbara

--

messages.subject: Re: comparing density estimates
messages.body_plain:
Barbara:

I don't believe ANOVA is what you want to do.  What exactly is the question you
wish to ask?  If the question is 'was density constant during the period
2001-2006,' you could probably assess this question by assessing trend in your
estimates (and their associated measures of precision).

I don't have the reference in front of me at home, but the reference I would
consult to address this question would be the chapter by Thomas, Burnham, and
Buckland in the Advanced Distance Sampling text of Buckland et al. (2004).
This chapter deals with addressing issues of spatial and temporal trends in
density estimates.

Quoting Barbara Franzetti <fran...@iperbole.bologna.it>:

Dear list,

I gathered point census data on songbirds. I calculated detection=20
functions stratified per study area, but since I need densities on a fine=
r=20
scale (per month), I decided to calculate these densities by hand, based=20=

on the detection functions from distance and the formulae found in=20
Buckland et al. 2001 chapter 2.

I try to understand how a uniform key function is like,but it is not=20
completely clear to me. For all other key and expansion functions, I=20
calculated a g(0) around 1, as required. However, when the detection=20
function uses a uniform key function, I always end up with small g(0)=20
values after calculation (0.05-0.1 instead of 1), although it is clear=20=

from the graph that detection probability at distance zer =3D 1. As I was=
=20
trying to understand the reason for this problem, I realized that I don't=
=20
understand the logic after the uniform key formula:

The uniform key function =3D 1/w (w=3D truncation width) (Buckland et al.=
 2001=20
p 47). How can the detection probability change according to the w chosen=
?=20

Is there maybe a mistake in this key formula or could somebody explain=20=

where I'm wrong?

Thanks a lot=20

Valerie Lehouck

estimate trend across years.  If the same points are surveyed each year i=

it more appropriate to use auto regression or timeseries approaches that=20=

address temporal autocorrelation?  For more complicated mixed models that=
